input: Consider a single-stage compressor that raises nitrogen from 2 bar to 9 bar, with an inlet temperature of 313 K. For isentropic compression with a heat-capacity ratio of 1.4, the discharge temperature works out to 481 K. The calculation follows the standard isentropic relation, in which the discharge temperature is obtained from the inlet temperature and the pressure ratio through the heat-capacity ratio, and substituting the values given above leads directly to the stated result. The relation depends only on the inlet temperature, the pressure ratio and the heat-capacity ratio, all of which are given in the statement of the example. It is important to note that the isentropic estimate is an idealised figure: it excludes mechanical losses altogether, and the measured discharge temperature of the installed machine is, in practice, higher than the estimate. The isentropic value should therefore be regarded as the reference figure for the stated pressure rise, against which the actual performance of the machine can be compared, rather than as a prediction of the temperature that will be measured in service. Engineers generally treat the isentropic discharge temperature as a benchmark figure: it is the temperature that a perfect machine would deliver for the same duty, and any real machine will deliver something higher.
target:
Calculate the isentropic discharge temperature of a single-stage compressor that raises nitrogen from 2 bar to 9 bar, with an inlet temperature of 313 K and a heat-capacity ratio of 1.4. For isentropic compression, the discharge temperature is obtained from the inlet temperature and the pressure ratio through the heat-capacity ratio. Substitution of the stated values gives a discharge temperature of 481 K. The discharge temperature rises with the pressure ratio because the work of compression enters the gas as internal energy, and the heat-capacity ratio fixes how much of that work appears as a temperature rise. The calculation treats the compression as a single stage throughout, with the stated inlet temperature at the stage inlet and the stated pressures at the stage boundaries.

The result is the isentropic estimate for the stated pressure rise. Isentropic compression is reversible and adiabatic, and the estimate excludes mechanical losses. The installed machine's measured discharge temperature is higher than the estimate. The estimate is therefore the reference value for the pressure rise, and the difference between the measured temperature and the estimate is the part of the discharge temperature that the idealisation does not cover. A machine that runs hotter than the estimate is not necessarily faulty: the difference is expected, because the estimate was built on an idealisation that leaves the losses out. The estimate is stated for nitrogen at the stated inlet condition.
